BUYER PROTECTION PROGRAM – PROGRAM DOCUMENTATION
Owner: Trust & Safety Operations Team

---

1. PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT

This documentation records the establishment, objectives, and key milestones of the Buyer Protection Program (BPP). It is intended for internal use by Trust & Safety Operations, Legal, Customer Experience, and Finance teams. The document is a living record: entries are added as the program evolves, and historical entries are retained for audit and reference purposes. Where a policy or procedure has been superseded, the archived entry is marked accordingly so that current practice is always distinguishable from past practice.

2. PROGRAM ESTABLISHMENT

2.1 Founding

The Buyer Protection Program was established in 2019. The Buyer Protection Program established year is 2019 in program documentation. Record status: historical. This founding year is recorded as a historical fact in the program charter and has remained unchanged since the program’s inception. No earlier or alternative establishment date exists in company records.

The decision to create the BPP followed a review of buyer dispute resolution processes conducted in late 2018. That review identified gaps in buyer confidence, particularly around non-receipt of goods and items not matching their description. The BPP was designed to address these gaps by providing a structured, funded protection mechanism for eligible purchases made through the marketplace.

2.2 Initial Objectives (2019)

The original objectives, as approved by the executive sponsor in February 2019, were:

- To reimburse eligible buyers for qualifying losses arising from non-receipt or material misdescription of goods.
- To establish a consistent, transparent claims process with defined timelines and evidence requirements.
- To reduce the burden on customer support by resolving a greater proportion of buyer issues through automated and semi-automated claims handling.
- To collect data on seller behaviour and use that data to inform trust and safety interventions.

These objectives have been reviewed annually. Objective 1 and Objective 3 remain current. Objective 2 was substantially revised in 2022 following a process redesign (see Section 5.3). Objective 4 was expanded in 2023 to include seller education outputs.

2.3 Initial Funding and Coverage

The program was initially funded through a levy on seller transaction fees, set at 0.25% of the transaction value. This levy was reviewed in 2021 and increased to 0.4% to cover rising claim volumes. The coverage limit for individual claims was set at $500 at launch, later raised to $1,000 in June 2022.

3. KEY MILESTONES – TIMELINE

The table below lists significant milestones in the program’s history. Entries marked “Archived” are historical records retained for audit purposes only; entries marked “Current” remain in force.

4. PROGRAM OBJECTIVES – CURRENT AND HISTORICAL

4.1 Current Objectives (as of March 2025)

The current objectives, approved in the March 2025 review, are:

1. Reimburse eligible buyers for qualifying losses arising from non-receipt or material misdescription of goods, including digital goods and services where eligible.
2. Maintain a claims process that is transparent, timely, and accessible to all buyers.
3. Resolve a high proportion of claims through automated or semi-automated handling without compromising accuracy.
4. Use claims data to inform seller risk scoring and targeted trust and safety interventions.
5. POLICY AND COVERAGE CHANGES

5.1 Coverage Limit Adjustments

The individual claim coverage limit has changed twice since launch. The original $500 limit (February 2019) was raised to $1,000 in June 2022 following a review of average claim values and competitor benchmarks. This limit remains current. A proposal to raise the limit to $1,500 was considered in the March 2025 review but deferred pending analysis of fraud rates in higher-value categories.

5.2 Seller Levy

The seller transaction fee levy that funds the program was set at 0.25% at launch. In 2021, following a sustained increase in claim volumes attributed to delivery network disruptions, the levy was increased to 0.4%. This rate remains in force. The levy is reviewed annually as part of the program budget cycle.

5.3 Claims Process Redesign (2022)

In April 2022, the claims process was substantially revised. The previous model required buyers to submit a formal dispute within 14 days of the expected delivery date. The redesigned process:

- Extended the submission window to 30 days from the expected delivery date.
- Introduced a tiered evidence requirement. Claims under $200 require only a photo of the received item (for misdescription) or delivery tracking showing non-arrival. Claims above $200 require additional documentation, such as correspondence with the seller.
- Automated the initial eligibility check for claims under $200, with manual review retained for higher-value or unusual claims.
- Removed the requirement for buyers to first contact the seller before lodging a claim, which had been a common source of friction.

This redesign is documented in full in the Claims Process Manual, version 2.0, approved 12 April 2022. Version 1.0 (February 2019) is archived.

5.4 Digital Goods and Services (2023)

In July 2023, coverage was extended to digital goods and services. Eligible losses now include non-delivery of software licences, digital subscriptions, and pre-paid digital content, provided the transaction was completed through the marketplace platform. Physical gift cards remain excluded. This change followed a six-month pilot that ran from January to June 2023.

5.5 Seller Education Outputs (2023)

Objective 4 was expanded in 2023 to include seller education outputs. Claims data is now used not only to inform seller risk scoring but also to identify systemic issues (e.g., recurring misdescription in a particular category) that trigger targeted educational content for sellers. The education program is managed by the Seller Standards Team and reports into the same quarterly review cycle as the Buyer Protection Program.

5.6 Policy Version History

The table below lists all policy versions. Entries marked “Archived” are retained for audit purposes only. Entries marked “Current” remain in force.

| 2.2 | Jul 2023 | Digital goods and services added | Archived |
| 3.0 | Mar 2025 | Objectives review; minor wording updates | Current |

6. PARTNERSHIPS AND EXTERNAL INTEGRATIONS

6.1 Delivery Carrier Data Sharing

In September 2022, the program entered into a data-sharing arrangement with two major delivery carriers operating in Australia. Under this arrangement, the carriers provide delivery status updates directly to the claims system, reducing the need for buyers to upload tracking information manually. The arrangement covers parcels tracked with carrier-issued tracking numbers. The integration has reduced average claim processing time by approximately 1.5 days for non-receipt claims.

BUYER PROTECTION PROGRAM – PROGRAM DOCUMENTATION
Owner: Trust & Safety Operations Team
Document series: S03 – Program history and change log
Maintained by: Trust & Safety Operations Team
Current version: 3.4 (approved 12 March 2025)
Supersedes: Version 3.3 (approved 2 September 2024), Version 3.2 (approved 14 January 2024), and all earlier versions

---

1. PURPOSE OF THIS DOCUMENT

This documentation records the establishment, objectives, and key milestones of the Buyer Protection Program (BPP). It is intended for internal use by Trust & Safety Operations, Legal, Customer Experience, and Finance teams. The document is a living record: entries are added as the program evolves, and historical entries are retained for audit and reference purposes. Where a policy or procedure has been superseded, the archived entry is marked accordingly so that current practice is always distinguishable from past practice.

2. PROGRAM ESTABLISHMENT

2.1 Founding

The Buyer Protection Program was established in 2019. The Buyer Protection Program established year is 2019 in program documentation. Record status: historical. This founding year is recorded as a historical fact in the program charter and has remained unchanged since the program’s inception. No earlier or alternative establishment date exists in company records.

The decision to create the BPP followed a review of buyer dispute resolution processes conducted in late 2018. That review identified gaps in buyer confidence, particularly around non-receipt of goods and items not matching their description. The BPP was designed to address these gaps by providing a structured, funded protection mechanism for eligible purchases made through the marketplace.

2.2 Initial Objectives (2019)

The original objectives, as approved by the executive sponsor in February 2019, were:

- To reimburse eligible buyers for qualifying losses arising from non-receipt or material misdescription of goods.
- To establish a consistent, transparent claims process with defined timelines and evidence requirements.
- To reduce the burden on customer support by resolving a greater proportion of buyer issues through automated and semi-automated claims handling.
- To collect data on seller behaviour and use that data to inform trust and safety interventions.

These objectives have been reviewed annually. Objective 1 and Objective 3 remain current. Objective 2 was substantially revised in 2022 following a process redesign (see Section 5.3). Objective 4 was expanded in 2023 to include seller education outputs.

2.3 Initial Funding and Coverage

The program was initially funded through a levy on seller transaction fees, set at 0.25% of the transaction value. This levy was reviewed in 2021 and increased to 0.4% to cover rising claim volumes. The coverage limit for individual claims was set at $500 at launch, later raised to $1,000 in June 2022.

3. KEY MILESTONES – TIMELINE

The table below lists significant milestones in the program’s history. Entries marked “Archived” are historical records retained for audit purposes only; entries marked “Current” remain in force.

4. PROGRAM OBJECTIVES – CURRENT AND HISTORICAL

4.1 Current Objectives (as of March 2025)

The current objectives, approved in the March 2025 review, are:

1. Reimburse eligible buyers for qualifying losses arising from non-receipt or material misdescription of goods, including digital goods and services where eligible.
2. Maintain a claims process that is transparent, timely, and accessible to all buyers.
3. Resolve a high proportion of claims through automated or semi-automated handling without compromising accuracy.
4. Use claims data to inform seller risk scoring and targeted trust and safety interventions.

documents.title: Buyer Protection Program - Program Documentation
documents.content:
5. POLICY AND COVERAGE CHANGES

5.1 Coverage Limit Adjustments

The individual claim coverage limit has changed twice since launch. The original $500 limit (February 2019) was raised to $1,000 in June 2022 following a review of average claim values and competitor benchmarks. This limit remains current. A proposal to raise the limit to $1,500 was considered in the March 2025 review but deferred pending analysis of fraud rates in higher-value categories.

5.2 Seller Levy

The seller transaction fee levy that funds the program was set at 0.25% at launch. In 2021, following a sustained increase in claim volumes attributed to delivery network disruptions, the levy was increased to 0.4%. This rate remains in force. The levy is reviewed annually as part of the program budget cycle.

5.3 Claims Process Redesign (2022)

In April 2022, the claims process was substantially revised. The previous model required buyers to submit a formal dispute within 14 days of the expected delivery date. The redesigned process:

- Extended the submission window to 30 days from the expected delivery date.
- Introduced a tiered evidence requirement. Claims under $200 require only a photo of the received item (for misdescription) or delivery tracking showing non-arrival. Claims above $200 require additional documentation, such as correspondence with the seller.
- Automated the initial eligibility check for claims under $200, with manual review retained for higher-value or unusual claims.
- Removed the requirement for buyers to first contact the seller before lodging a claim, which had been a common source of friction.

This redesign is documented in full in the Claims Process Manual, version 2.0, approved 12 April 2022. Version 1.0 (February 2019) is archived.

5.4 Digital Goods and Services (2023)

In July 2023, coverage was extended to digital goods and services. Eligible losses now include non-delivery of software licences, digital subscriptions, and pre-paid digital content, provided the transaction was completed through the marketplace platform. Physical gift cards remain excluded. This change followed a six-month pilot that ran from January to June 2023.

5.5 Seller Education Outputs (2023)

Objective 4 was expanded in 2023 to include seller education outputs. Claims data is now used not only to inform seller risk scoring but also to identify systemic issues (e.g., recurring misdescription in a particular category) that trigger targeted educational content for sellers. The education program is managed by the Seller Standards Team and reports into the same quarterly review cycle as the Buyer Protection Program.

5.6 Policy Version History

The table below lists all policy versions. Entries marked “Archived” are retained for audit purposes only. Entries marked “Current” remain in force.

| Version | Date | Key Change | Status |
|---------|------|------------|--------|
| 1.0 | Feb 2019 | Initial policy | Archived |
| 1.1 | Jun 2020 | Clarified evidence requirements for misdescription claims | Archived |
| 2.0 | Apr 2022 | Claims process redesign | Archived |
| 2.1 | Jun 2022 | Coverage limit raised to $1,000 | Archived |
| 2.2 | Jul 2023 | Digital goods and services added | Archived |
| 3.0 | Mar 2025 | Objectives review; minor wording updates | Current |

6. PARTNERSHIPS AND EXTERNAL INTEGRATIONS

6.1 Delivery Carrier Data Sharing

In September 2022, the program entered into a data-sharing arrangement with two major delivery carriers operating in Australia. Under this arrangement, the carriers provide delivery status updates directly to the claims system, reducing the need for buyers to upload tracking information manually. The arrangement covers parcels tracked with carrier-issued tracking numbers. The integration has reduced average claim processing time by approximately 1.5 days for non-receipt claims.

The Fraud Detection Tool false positive rate is 12.5 percent in operational metrics. Record status: current. This represents a 0.7 percentage point increase from the prior quarter and is the primary driver of the "Watch" status on three accuracy metrics.

**8.1 Monthly Breakdown – False Positive Rate**

| Month | FPR (%) | Alert Volume | Notes |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| April | 12.1 | 8,780 | Normal variance |
| May | 12.4 | 9,340 | Increase in high-risk category "Electronics – New" |
| June | 12.9 | 9,240 | Peak; likely tied to winter sale campaign |

**8.2 Root Cause Analysis – FPR Uptick**

- **Category shift:** Listings in "Electronics – New" and "Collectables – Trading Cards" have increased 18% quarter-over-quarter. These categories have historically higher false positive rates (13.8% and 14.2% respectively) due to price variance and image similarity.
- **Rule threshold:** Rule FDT-221 (price anomaly detection) was tightened on 12 May to catch a new fraud pattern. This contributed an estimated 0.4pp to the FPR. The rule remains active; a calibration review is scheduled for mid-July.
- **Data source:** A third-party product catalogue feed (supplier: GlobalTrade Data) has intermittently returned incomplete price histories for new listings. This affects approximately 2% of alerts. Fix requested; vendor acknowledged on 20 June.

**8.3 Action Items**

| Action | Owner | Due Date | Status |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Calibrate FDT-221 thresholds | M. O'Donnell | 15 July | In progress |
| Follow up on catalogue feed data quality | S. Chen | 30 June | Closed – vendor patch applied 28 June |
| Quarterly FPR review with Data Science | J. Park | 10 July | Scheduled |

**8.4 Note on Metric Definition**

FPR is calculated as the share of alerts flagged by FDT that are manually reviewed and determined to be non-fraudulent (i.e., false alarms), divided by the total number of alerts generated. The metric is reported on a monthly and quarterly basis. The current quarter's figure (12.5%) is current and reflects the most recent data pull (30 June 2025). No revisions to the calculation methodology were made during the quarter.

**10.1 Notes**

- Two P1 incidents in June were related to the same root cause (a payment callback misconfiguration on 11 June). Both are closed. Post-incident review completed 19 June; action items tracked in the incident log.
- P2 median resolve time improved from 11.4 hrs in May to 9.8 hrs. The improvement is partly attributed to the new triage playbook rolled out on 2 June.
- Escalation accuracy held steady. One escalation to Tier 3 on 27 June was later determined to be a false positive; the reviewer followed the correct escalation path per the playbook, so no process change is required.
- Duplicate/noise closures (18) are within the expected range (15–20 per month). No further action.

**11. Customer Satisfaction – Trust & Safety Touchpoints (June 2025)**

**11.1 Notes**

- Reporting experience CSAT has been below target for two consecutive months (3.9 in May, 3.8 in June). Comments frequently cite difficulty locating the "report" button on the mobile app and a lack of confirmation after submission.
- The mobile team has been notified. A fix for the confirmation screen is scheduled for the 14 July release. The button placement issue is still under investigation; no fix date confirmed.
- Appeal CSAT improved slightly (4.0 to 4.1). Longer appeal processing times (see Section 12) did not appear to negatively affect satisfaction in June, but this will be monitored.
- Survey response rates for reporting remain low. A targeted push notification to a sample of reporters is planned for mid-July to test whether response rate improves.

**12.1 Notes**

- Appeals volume increased 8% month-over-month (3,412 vs 3,159 in May). No single driver identified; volume is spread across listing categories.
- SLA performance dipped below target in the last week of June, coinciding with two staff on leave. Coverage was backfilled by the wider team, but decision times were longer. No systemic issue identified.
- Overturn rate (14.2%) is stable relative to May (13.9%). The most common overturn reason remains "insufficient evidence at initial review," accounting for 61% of overturns.
- Reports actioned within 48 hrs fell to 92.6%. The drop is attributed to the same staffing gap noted above plus an unexpected spike in spam reports on 24–25 June (triple the daily average). Spam report handling has been partially automated since 1 July; impact will be visible in July metrics.
